#7798. 2026’s Best Snow Blowers for Gravel Driveways, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Zach Lazzari, Tom Scalisi, Additional research provided by Tony Carrick

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Snow blowers for gravel driveways aren’t just any ol’ snow blowers. To ensure you clear snow without tossing rocks and dirt around your property, choosing the right type of snow blower for your gravel driveway or walkway is essential. To help you in your decision, we consulted a snow removal expert and tested eight popular snow blowers by plowing over packed and loose gravel.

Once our testing was complete, we chose the Troy-Bilt Storm Tracker 2890 Snow Blower as our top pick for its adjustable blade height, excellent traction on loose surfaces, and especially wide clearing path. Learn more about how this reliable snow blower machine and the rest of our recommendations performed in our tests, and see which features matter most when choosing among the best snow blowers for gravel driveways.

Bottom line: Choosing the right snow blower for gravel driveways is crucial. Our top picks offer a range of options for different needs and budgets.

Before purchasing a snow blower for a gravel driveway, it’s important to understand that not all machines will work for this type of surface. For example, most single-stage snow blowers and electric snow shovels have augers that scrape along the ground. While this design is great for snow removal from smooth pavement, sidewalks, and heated driveways, it doesn’t work well on gravel driveways since it will pick up gravel in addition to snow.

Still, there’s no need to resort to using a standard snow shovel. Two-stage and three-stage snow blowers have augers that operate an inch or so above the ground as well as adjustable skids that provide clearance to prevent the machine from scooping up gravel.

All of the selections listed below are suitable for gravel driveways. Our lineup includes both gas-powered and electric cordless snow blowers and features models for small and large driveways alike.

While keeping rocks out of spinning tines is crucial when snow-blowing a gravel driveway, getting traction on this loose material is also important, which is why the Storm Tracker 2890 is such an ideal option. The track system creates more surface contact with the ground than a set of wheels, leading to significantly more traction on icy inclines where tires tend to spin and struggle. Like other quality snow blowers designed to work on gravel surfaces, the Storm Tracker is equipped with adjustable skid shoes that create necessary clearance for the spinning auger blade.

Though it uses a standard skid system, the Storm Tracker amplifies it with an adjustable handle that raises and lowers the bottom blade height—a major differentiator for working safely on gravel. These adjustments prevent dirt and rocks from being ingested by the auger and allow users to gradually lower the blade when working through deep snow banks. In our tests, we found ourselves using the height adjustment frequently, but that wasn’t the only thing we liked about this model. The motor started on the first or second pull in cold conditions, and it fired up immediately using the electric start. All of the controls were easy to use, including excellent chute adjustment controls.

What our tester says: “We were very impressed with how useful this machine’s six forward-speed settings and two reverse speeds were. We could throttle down to a crawl or hit the high gears and really move. Everything about this model is made for heavy-duty snow-blowing, and it did not disappoint.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Read our full review: Troy-Bilt Storm Tracker 2890 Snow Blower

Get the Troy-Bilt snow blower for gravel driveways at Walmart or DK Hardware.

With a price tag that’s significantly less than many other snow blowers, this two-stage model from PowerSmart is a good snow blower for those looking to clear a gravel driveway without breaking the bank. As with other two-stage snow blowers, the PowerSmart’s auger uses skids to remain above the ground, ensuring it won’t pick up gravel as it goes. Its 180-degree chute is easy to control from the handles with one hand, enabling quick changes after each turn.

Not all affordable snow blowers offer the array of features found on top-rated machines, but the PowerSmart is quite competitive with what it includes. This model has a push-button electric start, an anti-clogging system, a self-propelling design, and 13-inch inflatable tires with traction. It also has six forward speeds and two reverse speeds, which helped us work through powder, wet snow, and icy snow without issue. It doesn’t quite have the traction and power of some more expensive models, but it’s more than ample for the average user.ction and power of some more expensive models, but it’s more than ample for the average user. We really enjoyed this unit and although it’s not the top choice, it does offer a great value for budget shoppers.

Get the PowerSmart snow blower for gravel driveways at Amazon or PowerSmart.

A blower for a gravel driveway should run efficiently, pivot quickly, and be capable of moving large snow loads in a single session, and the Toro Power Max 824 OE can do it all. We used the Toro to plow through a long stretch of hard-packed gravel road, clearing 6 to 8 inches of snow, and were amazed to see how much ground we covered simply by sliding the throttle to rabbit speed and setting the snow blower to the six-speed position. By the time a snow plow arrived, we’d already cleared a major section of the road.

While other top choices in this category have larger 28-inch-wide clearing widths, this 24-inch model is more than capable of clearing a long driveway that receives moderate snowfall with the occasional heavy storm. Like many Toro blowers, it has a joystick control for easy chute adjustments. It also features a convenient electric start, best-in-class chute controls, and a reliable engine, making it hard to go wrong with this model. Although we gave it the award for long driveways, it’s suitable for just about any snow removal need.

Get the Toro 824 OE snow blower for gravel driveways at Ace Hardware or Acme Tools.

Not surprisingly, the Toro Power Max e24 has many similarities to the Power Max 824 OE. In fact, the body, auger, and control designs are nearly the exact same. This makes sense because there is no reason to reinvent the wheel when Toro already offers exceptional controls, a durable steel auger, and a great set of features and functions.

The main difference is the motor. Rather than a gas engine, it has an all-electric motor powered by up to three batteries. While it can run on a single battery, adding a second extends the runtime up to 70 minutes, and a third extends it even more. We tested the snow blower with just one battery, and it performed exactly like the gas model for over 30 minutes before requiring a recharge.

There are plenty of great electric options on the market, but the advantages this one offers are why we awarded it the title of the best electric snow blower for gravel driveways. The fact that the steel auger doesn’t require shear pins is a major bonus since there’s nothing to break (and then replace) if the machine is under excess stress. Purchasing a third battery also makes it among the longest-lasting snow blowers on the market.

What our tester says: “We loved this snow blower’s performance and ability to churn through difficult snow. It was significantly quieter than the gas version, and because it’s both heavy duty and durable, it may well be the best electric snow blower available today.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer y to churn through difficult snow. It was significantly quieter than the gas version, and in large part because it’s both heavy duty and durable, we found it to be among the best electric snow blowers tested.

Get the Toro e24 electric snow blower for gravel driveways at Lowe’s or Acme Tools.

For those looking for a durable, all-around performance machine, the Husqvarna is a great option. The brand is known for its small engine-operated power tools, and this snow blower lives up to the high brand standards. In fact, we liked this 24-inch two-stage snow blower so much that we found it difficult to rank because it could have won almost any category on the list. It’s a solid unit made to work hard, and we were impressed with its combination of power and speed. Like every option we recommend, it has adjustable skids, a solid steel auger, and a powerful drive system.

The Husqvarna’s 212 cubic centimeter (cc) engine offers 5.9 horsepower, making it a good choice for gravel driveways with inclines. Its rugged tires offer excellent traction when working over icy surfaces, and we liked the user-friendly controls and good-size headlight for working in the dark. We loaned this model out to a local property management company to assist with a gravel driveway on a rural rental property, and they said it did a great job.durable, all-around performance machine, the Husqvarna is a great option. The brand is known for its small engine-operated power tools, and this snow blower lives up to the high brand standards.

Get the Husqvarna snow blower for gravel driveways at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Acme Tools.

While there are many top-rated snow blowers available today, not all are right for clearing a gravel driveway. When selecting the picks for our list, we stuck with models well suited for this type of terrain, namely two-stage blowers. Beyond type, we looked for features that make snow blowers easier to operate, such as push-button starters, heated handles, and sturdy materials that can power through packed snow.

We tested our selected models by clearing snow from multiple storms in rural Montana, using a loose-substrate gravel driveway and a hard-packed gravel road as our testing grounds. While much of the testing area was level, we also hit a few inclines and ran through mounds of piled-up snow.

We rated the snow blowers based on performance in each gravel environment. We looked at skids and adjustments that made it easier to run over gravel, and power, handling, and traction also factored high in the ranking process. Lastly, we assessed build quality, ease of use, battery life, engine performance, and the rest of the nitty-gritty details that make some snow blowers more capable on gravel surfaces.

Understanding which types of snow blowers are suitable for gravel driveways and which are not is the first step in selecting the right model. Ahead, learn more about the three types of snow blowers as well as other important features, such as power output and intake width.

There are three main types of snow blowers: single-stage, two-stage, and three-stage. Each one clears snow a bit differently, but for gravel driveways, two-stage models are ideal. Here’s how each of these snow blowers works.

Like all snow blowers, a single-stage snow blower or snow thrower uses an auger with serrated metal blades to scoop snow and launch it through the chute. Since the auger on this type of snow blower skims along the ground, it’s an excellent option for smooth pavement but a poor choice for loose gravel. If used on a gravel driveway, a single-stage snow blower will gather and throw rocks along with snow.

Similar to a single-stage snow blower, a two-stage model uses an auger to pull snow into the chute. However, rather than use the force of the auger to launch the snow, two-stage snow blowers rely on large impeller fans to propel the snow out of the chute. In addition to being able to throw snow much farther than a single-stage model, a two-stage snow blower’s auger does not come into contact with the ground. Instead of resting on the auger, the snow blower glides on two adjustable skid pads—a design that makes a two-stage model ideal for gravel surfaces.

This heavy-duty snow blower uses an auger and impeller fan along with an accelerator, which is  a corkscrew-shaped blade that sits perpendicular to the auger and pulls snow quickly into the machine as it spins. True to its name, an accelerator allows the machine to glide more quickly through snow. These powerful snow blowers can throw snow up to 50 feet away and have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide. This makes them ideal for covering large driveways. Like a two-stage snow blower, a three-stage model’s auger does not touch the ground, so it’s a good choice for gravel surfaces. Three-stage blowers also come with a hefty price tag. As such, they are typically only needed for regions that see very heavy snowfall.

When selecting a snow blower, consider how much power it needs to get the job done. Snow blowers have either a gas engine or, with battery-powered models, an electric motor. A gas snow blower’s power is measured in cubic centimeters. The higher the cc, the better able the snow blower is to move through deeper snow and the farther it can launch it. Two-stage snow blowers for gravel driveways have engines ranging between 200cc and 250cc.

Electric snow blowers generally use two batteries to maximize runtime, though many can run on one battery (but they won’t run as long). Total runtime varies depending on the voltage and amp hours of the batteries, the number of batteries used, and, of course, the amount and type of snow being cleared. Depending on these factors, many battery-powered snow blowers can run for between 30 and 70 minutes. Some electric snow blowers also have an additional port that enables adding a third battery to extend runtime.

Although battery-powered snow blowers may not be quite as powerful as gas-powered options, they operate at a much lower noise level and don’t produce exhaust fumes. They also don’t require periodic oil changes, making snow blower maintenance easier. Just keep in mind that lithium-ion batteries typically only last 3 to 6 years before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge, at which point they need to be replaced. Still, even replacing batteries may be less expensive than paying the cost of snow removal in areas that receive regular snowfall.

The width of the snow blower refers to the size of its intake and determines how broad a swath of snow the machine can remove with each pass. Most single-stage snow blowers remove snow in 11- to 22-inch swaths with each pass, making them suitable for small driveways and walks. Two-stage models range in width from 22 to 30 inches, making them ideal for most driveways. Large three-stage snow blowers have intakes that measure up to 40 inches wide.

Some of the best snow blowers for gravel driveways may come equipped with other useful features that make them easier and, in some cases, safer to use, such as:

In addition to buying a snow blower rated to work on gravel surfaces, there are other measures you can take to improve performance when clearing snow from this type of surface.

First and foremost, ensure the skid shoes—the two metal pieces that raise the snow blower intake and auger above the ground—are properly adjusted so that the intake is about 1 inch off the ground. This gap will provide enough clearance between the auger and the ground to prevent it from contacting the gravel.

If dealing with snow deeper than the height of the auger, consider raising the skid shoes to their highest setting to get the top layer of snow, then lower it to remove the remaining snow.

In windy conditions, start blowing upwind on the driveway and set the chute to discharge snow downwind. If the snow is particularly wet, adding nonstick snow blower spray to the chute can help prevent clogging.

When finished, make sure to clear any remaining snow from the auger to prevent it from freezing and clogging the intake.

Understanding the best strategy for removing snow with a two-stage snow blower and how to set it up to avoid throwing rocks is crucial when clearing a gravel driveway. Here is more information on proper use as well as some answers to common questions about snow blowers. two-stage snow blower and how to set it up to avoid throwing rocks is crucial when clearing a gravel driveway. Here is more information on proper use as well as some answers to common questions about snow blowers.

The best way to remove snow from a gravel driveway is to adjust the snow blower’s skid shoes to elevate its intake above the ground. This will prevent the machine from picking up and throwing gravel. If you don’t have a snow blower for your gravel driveway yet, check out our guide on clever hacks for how to shovel snow.

The best kind of snow blower to use on gravel is a two-stage model. The auger on a single-stage snow blower makes contact with the ground, so it will pick up gravel and throw it. A two-stage or three-stage snow blower has an intake that is elevated above the ground, allowing it to pick up snow without disturbing the gravel beneath it. Three-stage models work similarly, but they are heavy-duty options generally used by professionals.

They can last 10 years or many more if properly cared for. Snow blower maintenance includes changing the oil (for gas-powered models); lubricating the axle and augers; and periodically checking the shear pins, skid shoes, and belts for wear. Electric snow blowers require battery replacement about every 3 years if used regularly or up to 6 years if used intermittently.

The best time to get a good price on a snow blower is in either May or June, when manufacturers are introducing new models and demand for these winter-weather machines is low. If you need to buy outside this period, our guide on the best cheap snow blowers offers some excellent options.

We asked Thomas Vanneli, founder and CEO of Minneapolis, Minnesota’s Tomms Property Solutions, for advice on this problem. He said, “To avoid scratching concrete, rubber or polymer skid shoes should be installed. Skid shoes stop the metal from coming into contact with the concrete, which will protect it from dings and scratches.” You can also prevent damage to concrete surfaces by adjusting the skid shoes so the intake sits about an inch off the ground.

The snow blowers for gravel driveways we recommend in this guide cost between $600 and $1,900.

#7797. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

#7795. Blinds vs. Shades: How to Choose the Right Option for Your Home

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:57 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Blinds and shades are the two popular options, each with their own advantages in interior design and function. So, which one is right for your space? From design preferences and trends to the practical things like maintenance and insulation, we’ll take a look at the pros and cons of blinds vs. shades to help you find the perfect fit for your home.

Shades and blinds are both hung within (or just outside) the top of a window frame, and extend to the bottom of the glass pane, but the window coverings differ in the way they’re constructed. Blinds are composed of individual slats made from hard materials like wood, aluminum, or vinyl. These slats can be tilted to control the amount and direction of sunlight entering a room. Most blinds can also be raised or pulled to the side to fully expose the window.

Window shades, on the other hand, are generally made from a continuous piece of fabric or another flexible material that rolls, folds, or stacks when raised. They give a softer appearance and come in a variety of styles, from light-filtering roller shades to insulating cellular shades.

The right window treatment depends on more than just how they look. Before deciding between blinds and shades, consider how you use the room, how much natural light you want, and how much maintenance you’re willing to take on. These key factors can help narrow down your options.

Blinds.com’s premium roller shade blocks UV rays and preserves views, and is available in a variety of patterns, colors, and fabrics.

For precise control over how much sunlight gets through the window, blinds have the upper hand. The adjustable slats let you redirect sunlight up at the ceiling or away from a TV or computer screen, reducing glare while still keeping some natural light.

Shades are different. Light-filtering fabrics soften the harsh sunlight and give a gentle glow, while blackout shades are designed to block most incoming light. That said, shades don’t really let you fine-tune as much as blinds. For more flexibility, try top-down/bottom-up shades, which can be lowered from the top or raised from the bottom, or dual shades that use both light-filtering and blackout materials.

Cost for both blinds and shades will depend on the materials, size, and additional features. Basic vinyl or aluminum blinds tend to be the most budget-friendly options, so they’re practical if you’re looking to cover multiple windows without spending a fortune.

Shades can also be affordable, assuming you’re looking at simple roller shades made from synthetic fabrics. However, premium Roman shades, double-cell cellular shades, and custom fabric options will cost more.

For either option, custom sizing, professional installation, and motorized or smart controls can significantly inflate the price tag. Standard-sized, manually operated window treatments are usually the cheapest choice.

Window treatments can also help keep your home comfortable throughout the year. When it comes to insulation, however, certain types of shades have a clear advantage.

Cellular shades are particularly effective thanks to their honeycomb construction, which traps air in pockets between the window and the room. This helps reduce heat loss during winter and heat gain during summer, potentially lowering your energy bills. Roman shades with insulating liners can also provide some thermal benefits.

Blinds can help reduce solar heat gain by blocking or redirecting direct sunlight, but gaps between the slats don’t give you much insulation. If energy efficiency is one of your priorities, well-fitted cellular shades may be your best bet.

Older blinds and shades have long pull or loop cords, which are a serious strangulation hazard to young children and pets. Luckily, today’s options are much safer, with cordless designs becoming the standard for both blinds and shades.

There was even an update to window-covering safety standards in June 2024, which restricted hazardous cords on custom window coverings even more. Thanks to this change, you can now choose from a wide range of cordless and motorized options in both categories.

According to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, cordless window coverings are the safest choice for homes with young children. If you still have older cord-operated blinds or shades, replacing them with cordless alternatives is recommended.

These fabric vertical blinds from Blinds.com filter harsh sunlight and are durable, cost-effective alternatives to drapes.

Window treatments can have a surprising impact on the look and feel of a room. If you’re wondering how to dress a window without curtains, both blinds and shades give you plenty of stylish options. Blinds have a structured, tailored appearance that works well in modern, minimalist, and traditional interiors. Wood and faux wood blinds can add warmth and natural texture, while aluminum blinds look great in industrial or modern spaces.

Shades have a little more variety in terms of fabric, color, pattern, and texture. Roman shades can create an elegant, layered look, while simple roller shades are ideal for a clean, understated aesthetic. Woven wood shades made from bamboo or other natural materials can give organic texture and complement coastal, bohemian, or rustic spaces.

Of course, it will all come down to your own preference and the atmosphere you’re trying to create. Blinds are ideal for a crisp, structured look, while shades can make a room feel softer and more inviting.

In general, blinds are easier to maintain than shades. The hard surfaces are easy to dust or wipe down with a damp cloth, so they’re a great choice for kitchens, bathrooms, and other areas where moisture or splashes are common. Just keep in mind, though, that cleaning each individual slat can take time.

Fabric shades need a gentler approach. Most can be vacuumed with a brush attachment, while certain materials can be spot-cleaned. More delicate fabrics may need professional cleaning, and exposure to sunlight can cause some materials to fade over time.

In a busy house, low-maintenance blinds or easy-clean roller shades may be the most practical options.

WIth so many options, the material and configuration you choose can affect everything from durability to how much sunlight enters the room. Here are some of the most common types of blinds to consider:

Shades come in a huge range of styles, from simple designs to decorative options that can be more of a focal point in the room. Some of the most popular types include:

When choosing between blinds and shades, the decision comes down to what you want in your space. If precise light control, durability, and easy cleaning are your priorities, blinds are probably best. If you prefer a softer aesthetic, better insulation, or room darkening, shades may be worth the extra cost.

Remember, you don’t have to commit to one type of window treatments and use it throughout the home. Use blinds for high-traffic areas like kitchens and home offices, and shades for bedrooms and living spaces where comfort and aesthetics are more of a priority. Mixing and matching window treatments can help you strike the right balance between style, functionality, and budget.

#7794. GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

The garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

The garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

‘Tis the season…for family and friends to come crashing at your place for the holidays. The last thing a thoughtful host wants is for their guests to be uncomfortable, or feel unwanted and in the way. but let’s face it, the days of every homeowner having a dedicated spare bedroom to house guests are over.

Given the rise in remote work and home offices most homeowners no longer keep a full or queen bed “all dolled up” for company. (U.S. median home prices over $393,000 in the third quarter of 2026 might also mean that buying a home with an extra bedroom is cost prohibitive for many families.) For urban residents and apartment dwellers, the concept of “extra” space is a someday fantasy.

The good news is that no, your sister doesn’t have to sleep in your bathtub while she’s in town for the Thanksgiving parade. There are a number of creative ways you can squeeze extra sleeping space into your place, for the holiday season and beyond. From hidden beds and fold-out cots to child-friendly mats and mattresses, these are some of our favorite guest bed ideas for every budget.

Thank the Japanese for inventing the futon, the lightweight flexible mattress designed to be folded or rolled up, allowing a bedroom to be used for other purposes during the day. Traditional Japanese futons don’t have quite the same level as cushioning as Western sleepers tend to prefer, which has given rise to an entire category of convenient and comfy framed futons, including the Novogratz Tallulah Memory Foam Futon.

This classic vintage futon doubles as additional seating and features a sturdy wood frame, sleek wooden legs, button-tufted arms and back, and high-density foam and memory foam cushioning to provide support and comfort. The futon is upholstered in a soft velvet available in blue, grey, green and pink, and also features a split-back design that can be reclined independently to create multiple positions for lounging and sleeping.

Get the Novogratz Tallulah Memory Foam Futon at Wayfair for $669.99.

Multipurpose, multi-position, functional, and just plain fun, the Autlaycil sofa bed is a convertible chair, ottoman, lounger, and bed all in one compact package. Folded into an ottoman, it remains compact. And the backrest adjusts from 90 to 180 degrees for just the right angle for lounging. It’s available in seven colors.

Get the Autlaycil 4-in-1 Ottoman Chair Sofa Bed at Walmart, for $184.99.

For years, Murphy beds were the Rodney Dangerfield of the furniture industry: they “got no respect,” often serving as a punchline on old sitcoms. But in today’s space-crunched society, the Murphy bed is finally coming back into its own as a stylish and chic alternative way to provide extra sleeping space. This Night & Day Furniture Murphy Cube Cabinet Bed is a perfect example, giving the appearance of an attractive hardwood storage cabinet while concealing a queen-size bed complete with a 6-inch, trifold, premium gel memory foam mattress. When closed, the cabinet measures 36.6 inches high by 64.1 inches wide and 26.4 inches long, taking up just 10 square feet of floor space; open, it measures 25.7 inches high by 64.1 inches wide and 80.3 inches long.

Get the Night & Day Furniture Murphy Cube Cabinet Bed at Amazon for $1,897.

This Coleman Camping Cot, Air Mattress, and Pump Combo proves that you don’t have to be the outdoorsy type to enjoy quick and easy comfort, earning it a spot of honor in our researched guide to the best air mattresses. The air mattress itself is a supportive eight inches high when fully inflated, and the included folding cot raises the sleeping surface to 23.5 inches. The air mattress features a stable and supportive ComfortStrong Coil construction and an AirTight system with Double Lock valve to prevent the mattress from leaking. The included air pump operates on four D batteries. The sturdy steel cot construction can hold up to 300 pounds and accommodate sleepers up to 6 feet tall, yet weighs less than 14 pounds.

Get the Coleman Airbed Cot at Coleman for $220.99 (twin).

Sleeper sofas (or as your mom may have called them, hide-a-beds) have a lot of negative associations, including unattractive aesthetics for hosts and uncomfortable nights of tossing and turning for guests. But today’s sleeper sofas are a whole new world, as the Latitude Run Sleeper Sofa indicates. This storage-arm sofa combines an 87-inch long seating surface with a pull-out queen-size bed to accommodate more than one guest. The sofa bed is offered in a selection of three colors.

Get the Latitude Run 87-inch Upholstered Sleeper Sofa at Wayfair for $580.

Traveling with the little ones can be stressful enough without worrying about where they are going to be safe and secure while sleeping. Fortunately, the award-winning The Shrunks Toddler Travel Bed is easy to use, easy to transport, and features a special “guard rails and tuck” design that prevent the child from falling over the edge—standard-sized crib sheets and blankets tuck into the inner air mattress to keep the sleeper safe. The bed is sized specifically for children, at an inflated size of 60 inches long by 37 inches wide by 9 inches high. The package includes an electric pump that inflates the bed in 30 seconds, as well as a compact carry bag and a repair kit.

Get The Shrunks Toddler Travel Bed at Amazon for $69.99.

You would never guess that this Rebrilliant lounge chair also provides extra sleeping space. Velvet-feel upholstery goes with most all types of decor; caster wheels make it easy to move the chair around your space. It’s compact enough (31 inches high x 36 inches wide x 34 inches deep) for a studio apartment.

Get the Convertible Sleeper Chair at Wayfair for $379.99.

People of a “certain age” will definitely appreciate the height of this EnerPlex Double Height Inflatable Bed, as will anyone with back or knee problems that make getting down on the floor a nightmare. And space-constrained homeowners will love its compact size and the built-in dual pump that inflates the mattress in less than 2 minutes. When fully inflated, the twin-size mattress measures 80 inches long by 60 inches wide by 16 inches high, yet when deflated, the bed takes up no more room than a 1-foot-square package for easy storage.

The mattress is constructed of puncture-resistant PVC in a sturdy coil beam configuration, and also features a premium comfort top flocking to prevent leaking and provide non-slip stability. The combination of features, portability and reasonable price earned the EnerPlex the “best bang for the buck” designation in our researched guide to the best guest beds.

Get the EnerPlex Double Height Inflatable Bed w/ Built-in Dual Pump at Amazon, priced from $69.99.

Take a page from traditional Asian sleeping styles by providing guests with a firm but comfortable sleeping surface with the MAXYOYO Roll-Up Japanese Futon Mattress. Sleep on it, use it as as a floor lounger or even a yoga meditation mat—in any case, over 13,000 Amazon reviewers say it’s pretty comfy. Certified OEKO-TEX Standard 100 with a microfiber cover and 3.5-inch-thick, high-density foam filling, the mattress is available in a variety of colors and patterns, from cot-sized through king-sized. Roll it up and secure it with the accompanying straps and storage bag for convenient storage.

Get the MAXYOYO Japanese Floor Mattress at Amazon; twin priced from $82.

Offer your guests a combination of exceptional support and luxurious comfort with the Milliard Deluxe Diplomat Folding Bed, a practical and portable solution that was named the “best overall” product in our researched buyer’s guide to the best rollaway beds. The Milliard Diplomat Folding Bed features a full-steel, reinforced wire lattice frame that can handle up to 300 pounds. Its layered foam mattress incorporates a 3.5-inch supportive foam base and a cushy 1-inch memory foam top. The bed measures 75 inches long by 38 inches wide by 17 inches high, yet folds up into a slim, 14-inch profile on smooth-rolling wheels, allowing it to be tucked away in a closet when it’s not in use.

Get the Milliard Deluxe Diplomat Folding Bed at Amazon for $349.99.

If you prefer a traditional Japanese futon, it doesn’t get more authentic than the FULI Japanese Traditional Igusa (Rush Grass) Tatami Mattress. This classic hand-crafted tatami mattress is made by Japanese artisans from 100 percent rush grass (igusa) and serves as either a sleeping surface or a decorative floor covering. One benefit of sleeping on a classic tatami mattress is that it helps keep the back and body straight and the spine neutral. The lightweight tatami mattress weighs just 6.5 pounds and folds in thirds, allowing it to be tucked away easily when not in use.

Get the FULI Japanese Traditional Igusa Tatami Mattress at Amazon for $313.

Go from a casual chair to a cozy bed in short order with the CordayRoy’s Chenille Bean Bag Convertible Chair. In bean bag chair mode, it measures 42 inches around and 32 inches high to offer comfy sitting or sleeping with a small everyday profile. The full size bed measures 54 inches wide by 57 inches long and 8 inches high. When you’re done using the CordaRoy as a bed, fold it from the corners like a taco, pull the cover back over, then rotate, shake, and zip the bag closed. The cover for this fun piece of convertible furniture comes in a variety of colors to suit a living area, gaming room, or kid’s space.

Get the full size CordaRoy’s Chenille Convertible Bean Bag Chair at Amazon, priced from $329.99.

If your guest room doubles as an office, the Milliard Folding Mattress with Washable Cover, which provides an easy transition from daytime work to nighttime comfort. The 6-inch thick gel memory foam mattress was our top pick in our researched guide to the best foldable mattresses. It comes in several mattress sizes to sleep one or two guests, but folds up for easy storage. The full size mattress tri-folds to 12 inches by 52 inches by 25 inches. It comes with a jacquard carrying case to keep it clean while stored between uses or for camping.

Get the full size Milliard Folding Mattress with Washable Cover at Amazon for $199.99.

#7792. This $10 Hardware Store Staple Can Fix More Around the House Than You Think

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Donna Boyle Schwartz, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:32 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Caulk fixes myriad projects around the house, from outdoor maintenance to indoor decorating. What makes the material such a versatile DIY essential? The rubbery substance, available in a variety of formulations, including silicone, latex, acrylic, butyl rubber, polyurethane, and construction adhesives, can bond to almost any material, making it a wonderfully flexible material for projects indoors and out. With the right tube of caulk, you can solve just about any problem—including these common issues.

Caulking windows and doors is the best way to reduce drafts, cut home energy costs, enhance your house’s energy efficiency, and decrease your carbon footprint, according to the Consumer Federation of America. For this job, choose either acrylic latex or vinyl latex caulk. Acrylic latex caulk works best in dry environments and will perform well for up to 15 years, while vinyl latex can be used in damp areas and lasts about 5 years.

Concrete and mortar repair caulk is an excellent tool for sealing cracks and gaps in concrete, brick, stucco, stone, and metal. Similarly, it’s perfect for repairing small fissures in foundations and basement walls that allow insects, rodents, and other pests to enter your home. Designed for both interior and exterior use, concrete and mortar repair caulk has a textured finish and can be painted once it’s dry.

No matter how carefully you measure and cut, you often end up with little gaps between, above, and below moldings and baseboards. When you need to close the gap, acrylic latex caulk is one of the best caulks for baseboards, ideal for filling in those small spaces. The product dries quickly and can be painted as soon as 6 to 8 hours after application. Acrylic latex also comes in a variety of different pigments, so you can match the color to the surrounding material.

Over time, small spaces can open up between tiles, and in moist environments that’s an invitation for mold and mildew to grow behind the walls. Both 100 percent silicone caulk and siliconized acrylic caulk are ideal for wet environments and form a durable, watertight seal. Mold- and mildew-resistant silicone caulk is made for nonporous surfaces like ceramic, glass, and metal, while waterproof siliconized acrylic caulk works well on tubs, tile, glass, and ceramic tile surfaces. Gorilla silicone sealant is ideal to use since it is waterproof, and mold and mildew resistant.

Gorilla silicone caulk is flexible, adheres well, and creates a mold- and mildew-resistant barrier on bathroom surfaces. Read the review.

When you need to cover small holes and tiny cracks prior to painting, painter’s caulk, an acrylic latex compound, is just what you need. Painter’s caulk such as DAP Alex painter’s caulk adheres to wood, drywall, masonry, and other surfaces. Because it dries to a paintable texture in about an hour, it’s a good choice for busy DIYers.

Fire barrier sealant, a specialized type of caulk, does more than patch holes. It actually helps make your home safer by preventing fire from moving through open spaces within a structure. Fire barrier sealant can be used to seal holes, gaps, and cracks around holes in interior framing, especially around plumbing or electrical conduits.

When a length of molding falls off, a corner of carpet comes up, or a tile comes loose, all-purpose caulk can often fix it. Dab a little caulk behind the loose piece, then stick it back into place. You can even use an all-purpose caulk like GE all-purpose silicone caulk to install wood wall paneling without nails.

To keep wallpaper from pulling up as it dries, run caulk along all trimmed paper seams, especially in the corners, then smooth with a wet sponge or finger to remove any surface imperfections. For wallpaper that is peeling, lift up the loose section of paper, apply adhesive under it, then smooth the paper back against the wall. Once the adhesive dries, apply a continuous bead of caulk along the seam to keep it from peeling up again.

With the right caulk, you can even repair a roof! Roof repair caulk, like Roofers Choice Roof Cement Caulk, can be used to seal small cracks or gaps along roof edges, between shingles, and around skylights or flashing. As you might expect, roof repair caulk is completely weatherproof and waterproof, and can be used in wet areas or on dry surfaces.

As your home’s gutters age, they can develop cracks and gaps, especially around joints and downspout junctions. Butyl rubber caulk, a strong waterproof sealant, can be used to seal joints in those damaged gutters. Dab a little onto the cracks to keep your gutters leak-free—and keep rainwater flowing out and away from your home.

Painter’s caulk (or decorator’s caulk) is used, as its name suggests, just before decorating and painting. It’s the right choice for sealing crown molding, chair rails, and baseboards because it’s flexible and hides gaps between the wall and the finishes.

Whether you’re repairing a small hole or a sizable tear in your home’s vinyl siding, siding caulk can help. Simply choose a shade of exterior caulk that matches the hue of your exterior (even black caulk is available), and use a small dab to seal minor punctures, like nail holes. Cover larger holes or tears by applying caulk to the back of a scrap piece of siding, and covering the hole with the scrap piece.

Caulking between a countertop and a tile backsplash in the kitchen doesn’t just give your work space a “finished” look. It keeps crumbs, food items and worse yet, water, from getting behind your countertop and cabinets. Silicone caulk, which is moisture and mildew resistant, is the best caulk for the job. While you have your caulk gun out, make sure there’s a sturdy seal between your countertop and kitchen sink, too!

When you don’t have any fluffy furniture pads on hand to stick on the undersides of flower pots and other decorative items, caulk can help. Turn your pots on their sides and apply a few dabs of silicone caulk to the bottoms of the pots. Allow the caulk to dry so the pots won’t stick to your floors. When they’re set, the silicone pads should keep the pot from scratching your hardwood.

One of the easiest ways to keep your asphalt or concrete driveway in good condition is to attend to cracks as soon as you notice them. The longer you wait, the better the chance that moisture will seep into the cracks, and make an even more fractured-looking mess of your driveway. Load your caulk gun with a quality, water-resistant asphalt crack sealant. Acrylic formulas are flexible and should fit into just about any nook or cranny.

#7791. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options

Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

#7789. Arianne and Micah’s Small Urban Minneapolis Garden

Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

To submit, fill out the Garden Photo of the Day Submission Form.

You can also send 5–10 photos to [email protected] along with some information about the plants in the pictures and where you took the photos. We’d love to hear where you are located, how long you’ve been gardening, successes you are proud of, failures you learned from, hopes for the future, favorite plants, or funny stories from your garden.

#7788. It’s Not Too Late to Do the Lawn Maintenance You’ve Been Putting Off

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:11 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Many people assume lawn care ends when summer does, but autumn is when you’re laying the groundwork for next year’s success, says Allison Koenig, lawn and garden expert at Tractor Supply Company. “The work you do before winter, from mowing and fertilizing to leaf management and soil care, has a much bigger impact on spring performance than most homeowners realize,” she says. We spoke to Koenig and other lawn care experts to learn which fall lawn maintenance tasks you can still do even into early winter to improve the health and appearance of your lawn next spring, and what should be put off because it’s too late.

Earning perfect scores for ease of use, accuracy, and value in our hands-on test, this simple kit can help inform your fall lawn care routine.

The biggest misconception about fall lawn maintenance is that the lawn is dead because of cooler temperatures and doesn’t need attention anymore, says Koenig. But this isn’t true; the lawn is just dormant, which is a big difference. “A dormant lawn is still relying on the roots and reserves it built up in fall,” says Koenig. “Treat it like it’s done for the year and skip the prep work, and you’ll feel that mistake in spring.” Just be mindful that once the ground freezes or grass is fully dormant, it’s best to avoid aggressive projects like aerating, heavy raking, and major repairs. Winter is better spent protecting the lawn rather than trying to renovate it.

Pay a little attention to your lawn in fall and gain the rewards come the busy spring season. Experts suggest the following:

One of the simplest yet most important tasks in fall and winter is to keep your lawn free of debris, says Theresa Smith, senior vice president at NaturaLawn of America in Frederick, Maryland. “Fallen leaves and sticks can smother the grass, block sunlight, and trap moisture, leading to the grass becoming weak and susceptible to disease.” Regularly rake, mulch, and remove any large debris from the lawn to allow your grass to breathe and absorb as much sunlight as possible.

Mowing the lawn to the right height before winter arrives is an essential fall lawn task for preventing damage, says Smith. “Avoid cutting the grass too short, as this can lead to scalping and weakening the much-needed root system that it needs to survive winter,” she explains. “On the other hand, leaving the grass too long can also damage a lawn if it gets matted down with snow and ice, which can lead to disease and dying off.”

Fall is one of the most effective times for weed control because many weeds are moving nutrients into their roots as they prepare for winter, which makes them more susceptible to treatment, says Brian Feldman, lead agronomist and senior director of technical operations at TruGreen. Consider the timing and the type of lawn, though. “For cool-season lawns, the ideal window is generally October through early November, while warm-season lawns can still benefit from treatment later in the fall, particularly for certain winter annual weeds,” says Feldman.

Before you put down any fertilizer or aerate, Wells Westmoreland, co-founder of Tomball Lawn Care Service in Tomball, Texas, recommends getting a soil test first. “The results tell you exactly which nutrients your lawn is missing (or has too much of), so when you go to buy fertilizer or hire someone to apply it for you, you’re getting the nutrients your yard actually needs,” he explains.

Fall can be a great time to aerate and overseed your lawn; however, the best time of year depends on the type of grass you have. “Cool-season grasses, such as Kentucky bluegrass or tall fescue, should be aerated and reseeded in late summer through fall, or mid-August to mid-October,” advises Smith. On the other hand, warm-season grasses, such as zoysias and Bermuda grasses, should be aerated when they are more actively growing, usually during late spring or early summer.

After a hot and dry summer, lawns begin to recover in the early fall, making it an ideal time to apply fertilizer in support of its growth, says Smith. “Since daylight hours are shorter, the grass produces less top growth and directs the nutrients in the fertilizer toward root development, which helps keep the lawn healthy during colder months and helps yards that were fertilized to green-up quicker come springtime.” Some states have specific fertilizer restrictions in the late fall months, so be sure to check your state’s regulations before applying fertilizers.

Although winter typically reduces pest activity, some issues can still arise. Mice, voles, and other small mammals may take refuge in your lawn during the colder months, causing damage by burrowing or feeding on grass roots, warns Smith. “Check for signs of pest damage and act, such as using traps or deterrents if necessary,” says Smith. “Similarly, look for any patches where the grass has turned brown and may be holding disease spores. Rake up the dead grass and bag it so it doesn’t spread before winter temperatures arrive.”

Your grass doesn’t need nearly as much water this time of year, so decrease the frequency with which you water it. While you don’t need to stop, it’s a good time to pull back to avoid overwatering, which can cause large patches of your lawn to die off and invite fungus, disease, and root rot, says Westmoreland. “We see this a lot when sprinkler systems are still running on their summer schedule, so be sure to check your timer.”

It’s critical to avoid sodding during colder months. “You’ll likely spend several hundred dollars or more hiring a contractor, and the new sod has a very low chance of taking root because it can’t establish itself in the cold,” warns Westmoreland. Instead, wait until spring and you’ll get a much better return on that investment.

Adding a lot of nitrogen right before the cold months encourages new growth to pop up. “The problem here is that new growth gets hit harder by the cold than more established turf, so nitrogen can end up killing off a big chunk of your lawn,” explains Westmoreland. “Save the nitrogen for when things warm back up; then, the new growth will be supported.”

If you have a warm-season grass like St. Augustine, Bermuda, or zoysia, hold off on aeration and dethatching. These types of grasses only benefit from these processes when temperatures are much higher, as they’ll actively be growing during that time, says Westmoreland. “In the cold, the root zone on these grass types goes dormant, so aeration will just open up the turf to damage from the cold since the roots won’t be spreading as quickly.” However, if you have cool-season grass like fescue or ryegrass, you can still move forward with these tasks.

Once soil temperatures have dropped and winter conditions have arrived, it is most likely too late to overseed cool-season lawns, says Feldman.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.
