#7728. Who Is Left On The Bench For 2033?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Even if a Republican wins the 2028 presidential election, it will be virtually impossible for the Senate to flip red during his term. In all likelihood, there will not be a Republican President with a Republican Senate until 2033. As a result, it is unlikely that any conservatives are appointed to the Supreme Court, or the lower courts, over the next six years. A friend suggested, mostly in jest, that Chief Justice Roberts should resign to allow his seat to be filled during divided government. But I suspect the Democrats would just keep the seat open for two, four, even six years.

Ed Whelan writes, "The number of current Trump appellate appointees who will be 55 or younger in 2033 will be 18, and only 6 of those will be 50 or younger." Here is my (approximate) list of judges who Trump circuit appointees who were born after 1977. The six judges in blue at the end are the only ones who would be under 50--none from Trump's first term.

Of course, this all assumes there is no Court "reform" and there will still be a Supreme Court to worry about in six years.

I would make one other observation. Several of the judges who are accused of "auditioning" will likely age out of the Supreme Court short list by 2033. Can we finally exit the audition trap? Let's treat each opinion they write as a reflection of their best judgment, and not some attempt to secure higher office.

#7727. Propane vs. Gas Generators: Pros and Cons

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 16, 2026 12:37 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages are a common problem during thunderstorms, so it’s a good idea to have a backup plan ready to go when the lights go out. Gas and propane generators are common choices for home backup power, RV use, and camping trips.

Propane generators, for example, burn cleaner than gasoline generators, but tend to be more costly to purchase and operate. Gasoline generators are more efficient, but the fuel has a shorter shelf life and may not always be available in emergencies due to panic buying at local gas stations. This guide outlines other differences between the two that will help you decide which type of generator is right for your home.

Having a basic understanding of how the different types of generators work can help decide on the right choice for your home. A propane generator operates by burning the propane in an internal combustion engine. This process creates mechanical energy, which is used to turn a rotor within a magnetic field to generate electricity that can then be used to power appliances and other electronic devices.

Choosing a propane emergency generator for the home makes it easier to stockpile fuel for emergencies. Ken Goodrich, Founder and CEO of Kenerator, says “Propane is a great option for home backup power because it stores well and burns clean. Even when natural gas is temporarily shut off due to a natural disaster or infrastructure damage, a propane tank will continue to supply power.” Additionally, propane burns cleaner than gasoline, so you can expect the best propane generators to require less maintenance and produce fewer emissions.

Understanding how much propane a generator uses is key to deciding on the right model for your home, since propane generators tend to have lower fuel efficiency than gasoline generators. “Additionally, propane suppliers usually deliver to customers on a routine basis, so the homeowner needs to ensure they have enough propane to make it through an average outage,” notes Goodrich. It should also be mentioned that propane generators typically cost more up front and have higher operating costs, so they may not be the best choice for those looking for a cheap solution.

Whether you are looking to purchase a gas or propane generator, it’s good to know how the appliance operates. Generally, the operation of a gasoline generator can be described as a process that converts chemical energy into mechanical energy, which in turn produces electrical energy. More specifically, the engine burns gasoline to spin a shaft, which rotates magnets or electromagnetic fields near the stator, a stationary coil of wires. This induces a change in the magnetic field, creating an electrical current in the coils, that can then be used to power connected appliances and electrical devices.

The main benefit of a gas generator is that these appliances are more affordable to purchase and operate than propane generators, though there can be some fluctuation in the energy efficiency between specific models, so don’t hesitate to ask how much gas does a generator use when researching potential products.

Goodrich mentions that “portable gasoline generators are good options for camping and construction sites,” so you can make use of your generator even when you aren’t at home. Goodrich goes on to say that “gasoline generators are affordable, portable, easy to find, and simple to use,” making them a great choice for just about any home.

While gasoline generators may be cheaper to purchase and operate, gas does not burn as cleanly as propane, so there is a higher risk that these appliances will break down or require frequent maintenance to keep them in good condition. “Gasoline engines use carburetors, as opposed to mixers, which clog easily if not run on a weekly or monthly schedule,” Goodrich points out.

If you like the potential of both propane and gasoline generators, but can’t decide between one or the other, then you may find the best dual-fuel generators to be a good alternative. These generators work by switching between gasoline and propane using a manual or automatic fuel selector.

While the engine has the same combustion cycle for both fuels, it utilizes a built-in carburetor to atomize gasoline for combustion, but when using propane, the fuel passes through a separate external line and regulator before it is pulled into the engine by the vacuum created by the piston. Goodrich says that dual-fuel generators are “definitely a viable option. A lot of homeowners like having propane for its clean burn and long storage life, with gasoline as a backup if they run through their propane supply.”

Westinghouse iGen4500 has a 3.4-gal. gas tank that can run quietly for up to 18 hours; has a variety of ports but weighs 100+ lbs. Read the review.

Propane generators use safer, easier to store, and cleaner-burning fuel than gasoline generators; gas generators are more affordable to purchase and operate, with better fuel efficiency. “For most homeowners looking for reliable backup power, propane is the better long-term solution. That said, if you’re looking for something more budget-friendly, gasoline can still get the job done,” says Goodrich.

After gaining a basic understanding of the pros and cons between propane vs. gasoline generators, it’s a good idea to start your search by reading up on the best generator brands, then researching individual products that offer the features you want. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, a dual-fuel generator, powered by propane and natural gas, will offer you the best of both worlds so you are prepared for any emergency.

#7726. Judge Richard Posner, RIP

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, a founder of law and economics, and an enormously influential judge.

Judge Richard Posner passed away yesterday. Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, one of the founders of the field of law and economics, and probably the most influential lower-court federal judge of the last several decades. His contributions across a wide range of fields are so great, that no obituary can possibly do them justice.

As a longtime professor at the University of Chicago Law School, Posner was a pioneer of the application of economics to legal issues. His book Economic Analysis of Law, (which has gone through numerous editions since the first one in 1973), was and is the best overview of the field. His classic articles on antitrust law, regulation, the economics of common law, and many related issues were pathbreaking applications of economics to law that continue to influence economists, legal scholars, and policymakers even many decades later.

In addition to his many contributions to law and economics, Posner also published enormously influential books and articles on a dizzying array of other issues. I can only mention a few here. His book Sex and Reason is a tremendously insightful analysis of legal regulation of intimate relationships. How Judges Think and Reflections on Judging shed light on a variety of issues relating to judicial behavior, and legal philosophy. Law and Literature is one of the greatest books on the depiction of law in classic literary works. This list of pathbreaking Posner works can be extended almost endlessly!

Posner became a federal appellate judge in 1981 (appointed to the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit). There, he became perhaps the most influential federal lower court judge of his time, writing a variety of widely cited opinions. He was famous in legal circles for drafting almost all of his opinions himself, rarely relying on law clerks to do it.

A few of my own experiences with Posner and his work may shed some small additional light on the man and his achievements.

As a first-year law student, I was required to take an early-morning Contracts class. Not being a morning person, I periodically overslept and missed class (Posner, I'm sure, would never have done such a thing!). As a result, I was confused about some issues when final exam time came around. The class textbook was only of limited help in clearing up my confusion. So I decided to read the contracts chapter of Economic Analysis of Law. In a relatively few pages, Posner made everything much clearer, and I came to a much better understanding of a wide range of contracts issues than I had before, from studying the much longer textbook. Thanks to Posner, I did much better on the exam than I had any right to expect. He had a gift for distilling complex issues of law and public policy and making them readily understandable even to late-sleeping slackers!

A few years later, I was a law clerk for a federal appellate judge. Usually, when courts cite legal precedents, they do not indicate the name of the judge who wrote the decision. But my judge - who is more conservative than Posner and has a very different judicial philosophy - made clear that, when citing a Posner opinion, I should make sure to indicate Posner was the author. It's a small, but telling, indication of the respect Posner commanded from jurists across the political and jurisprudential spectrum.

Early in my academic career, I was co-editor of the Supreme Court Economic Review. One of the more difficult duties of academic journal editors is dealing with peer reviewers, who often procrastinate,  submit inadequate reviews, or both. One time, on a Friday afternoon, I e-mailed Posner an article submission, asking him to review it. Due to his simultaneous work as legal scholar and judge, Posner was almost certainly much busier than most of our other reviewers. Still, on Saturday morning, I woke up to find a message from Posner in my e-mail inbox. I expected the message would indicate whether he accepted the assignment or not. But instead, I found an extremely thorough and insightful review of the article I had sent him - one of the best peer review reports I have ever seen. In addition to his many other achievements and talents, Posner was extraordinarily hard-working and efficient. He made most of the rest of us seem lazy and indolent by comparison.

I was privileged to know Posner over a period of many years, though we interacted only occasionally. Most of my professional writings related to his work were critical, as in the case of my review of his book Law, Pragmatism, and Democracy, (to which he wrote a solid response,  and I in turn did a short rejoinder), and my criticism (in my book The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain) of his defense of the Supreme Court's controversial ruling in Kelo v. City of New London.

In retrospect, I fear these writings did not always sufficiently convey the enormous respect - even awe - that I had for Posner's many achievements. But I did support his longstanding campaign to get rid of the Bluebook, the ridiculously overcomplicated system of legal citation. In general, I am not a fan of book-burning. But I was happy to follow Posner in making an exception for the Bluebook! For a time, we even collaborated on an effort to persuade law journal editors to rethink the system.

Much, much more can be said. No words of mine can even come close to doing justice to Judge Posner's many achievements, or to his generosity to students and younger colleagues, of which my own experiences with him were just small examples. Thus, I will close by offering my profound condolences to those of his friends, family, and colleagues, who might read this post.

#7725. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

I was very pleased to see that Elliot Gaiser was nominated to the Federal District Court for the Northern District of Texas. I've seen some suggestions that Elliot does not have sufficient ties to Texas to support the nomination. Federal district court judges are required to live in their district upon confirmation. Indeed, I can think a number of recent appointees who have been nominated to courts in districts where they did not live in, and may not have lived in since their childhood.

Still, I think it may be useful to lay out some of Elliot's ties to my adopted home state of Texas. You see, not all of us were fortunate enough to be born in Texas, but we all got here as quickly as we could.

For starters, I've known both Elliot and his wife Alexandra since before they started dating. He was at the University of Chicago and she was the University of Texas. (I spoke at both of their FedSoc chapters while they were students.) Indeed, Elliot and Alexandra started dating long distance with knowledge that they would both be clerking in Houston--Elliot for Judge Edith Jones and Alexandra for Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod. I got to know both of them even better during their clerkship year.

Elliot's grandma has lived in Houston since Elliot was a child. Alexandra's immediate family is in Dallas, including her parents, brother, sister, and more. Alexandra's dad, Allen Harrison, is the president of Medical City Dallas and is the incoming chair of the Texas Hospital Association. Elliot and Alexandra were married in Texas, and their children were dedicated at that same chapel.

After clerking for Judge Jones, Elliot was at the D.C. Office of Gibson Dunn, and worked closely with the Dallas office. Elliot was on the briefing with James Ho and the First Liberty Institute for Sause v. Bauer before the Supreme Court. Elliot also worked on the Indian Child Welfare Act litigation in the Northern District of Texas. He represented Texas families who were seeking to adopt children of Indian descent. Elliot worked on the case in Judge Reed O'Connor's courtroom in the Northern District of Texas and before the Fifth Circuit. That case was also litigated in Texas State Court. In the Interest of Y.J. (also referred to as Y.R.J.), a Child, Trial Court Cause No. 323-107644-18, 323rd District Court, Tarrant County, Texas (Honorable Alexander Han Kim / Judge Alex Kim). Elliot also worked with the Dallas-based trial team at Gibson Dunn in the AT&T/TimeWarner antitrust suit.

Elliot and Alexandra have been closely connected to the Texas conservative legal movement. Alexandra interned for Sen. Cornyn's judiciary committee staff under Chief Counsel Matt Johnson and later Chief Counsel Noah Phillips. Alexandra is on the Steering Committee of the Texas Review of Law & Politics, where she served as Editor in Chief. Alexandra and Elliot are regular attendees at the annual TROLP banquet dinners. (Both of the Texas Senators are recipients of the coveted "Jurist of the Year" bobblehead, though mine is the most glamorous.) Elliot has spoken at the Texas Chapter Conference, and routinely attends Texas FedSoc happy hours and other gatherings.

Elliot is deeply respected by members of the Texas conservative legal movement. This evening, he attended the Texas FedSoc gathering at the Mayflower and we are all pulling for him. He would make a stellar judge and fill a seat that cannot be left empty.

#7721. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

#7716. Elon Musk Is Pulling the Plug on Cybertrucks to Focus on Something New

Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

Tesla hasn’t said which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The company plans to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the company can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

#7715. 14 Things You Can Do Now to Prepare for a Power Outage in Winter

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 16, 2026 5:18 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages can be difficult to weather any time of year, but not having a working heater when temperatures are frigid can be hard on you and your home. When there’s a winter storm in the forecast, there’s no time to lose. If you start preparing for inclement weather now, even before there’s a whisper about bad weather, and you’ll be in better shape should blizzards, nor’easters, or bomb cyclones head your way.

Make sure you have a good supply of batteries (and if they’re rechargeable batteries, ensure that they’re fully charged!) in a range of sizes for all your emergency needs. Have spares ready for flashlights and radios as well as for smoke detectors, clocks, and other necessities that can run on battery backup.

How many times have you clicked on several flashlights in your junk drawer before finding one that actually works? Carefully test each of your flashlights and figure out which ones work and which don’t. Refresh the batteries and test them again, ditching the flashlights that still don’t work. Purchase additional flashlights if you need them (can you really have too many?). Make sure there’s a “good” light for each member of the family, at the very least. Don’t plan on using candles; flashlights are safer.

Always top off your cars’ fuel tanks when you’re expecting a big storm. Gas station pumps run on electricity and if the power goes out, you won’t be able to get gasoline. If you have a gas-powered portable generator, fill some gas cans, too, so you can keep the generator going.

A key component of a winter survival kit is a means of charging your mobile phone in your car, whether that’s a car charger for your phone or the right cord to connect auto to phone. With a full gas tank and a car charger, you’ll be able to keep your phone working even if you lose power for an extended period of time. You may also want to invest in a solar phone charger, which would allow you to charge your phone without sitting in your driveway.

If you have landline telephone service, it’s worth keeping an old corded landline phone around. Modern phones that plug into wall outlets will not work during a power outage, and having access to a usable landline will help you conserve your cell phone battery.

If the power goes out during winter, how will you keep warm? Devise a plan now, before you’re in that situation. Even a gas-powered furnace requires electricity to run the fan that sends warm air through the vents. If you have a gas fireplace, consider installing a battery backup for the starter if you don’t already have one. If you rely on a wood stove for heat, stock up on firewood. Do not use a propane heater inside the home unless it is one specifically designed for indoor use; carbon monoxide can build up and create a deadly hazard.

Mr. Heater’s Portable Buddy Heater quickly heats up to 225 sq. ft. of space and has a tip-over safety mechanism. Read the review.

When a heavy storm is in the forecast, stock up on drinking water, and fill up the bathtub and washing machine so you’ll have enough water for washing and for flushing the toilets. The PennState extension service says Americans use 50 to 100 gallons of water per person per day, but that kind of stockpile may be hard to achieve in an emergency situation. You will want to have on hand at least a gallon of potable water per person per day.

If your home relies on municipal water, your water taps will keep flowing in the event of a power outage. But homes on well water aren’t so lucky—well pumps won’t work without electricity.

How will you cook if you lose electricity? If you have gas appliances, you should be able to light the pilot light with a match if you lose power. But if you have an electric stovetop and oven, you won’t be able to use your stove. You can, however, use a propane grill or an open fire to cook outdoors. If that’s your plan, refill the propane tank, or buy a cord of wood. And whatever your appliance situation, make sure you have a manual can opener.

Lowering the temperature of your refrigerator and freezer before the storm hits will help them stay cooler longer if the power goes out, thus increasing the likelihood that your food will be safe to eat after the power outage. Consider moving perishables like milk and meat into the freezer so they’ll stay colder. To conserve the cold air inside, avoid opening the refrigerator doors more than you absolutely have to.

If a winter power outage lasts more than a few days, you may run out of fresh food (or a means to prepare food). For this reason, it’s a good idea to keep plenty of nonperishable foods with long shelf lives like nut butters, canned fruit and juices, granola bars, and crackers on hand to keep yourself nourished.

Radios may seem a relic of the past, but these old-fashioned devices may just save your bacon if you lose power for an extended period. When modern methods of emergency alerts such as TVs and phones are offline, an emergency radio with fresh batteries may be your lifeline to news and information about dangerous conditions, even evacuation alerts. Better yet, select a radio can be charged in multiple ways. The Eton Odyssey radio, for example, can be charged via hand crank, USB-C, solar, and rechargeable and alkaline battery.

The Midland WR120B can be programmed to check weather in 25 local regions, so you can stay on top of loved ones’ forecasts Read the review.

Loss of power could be an excuse for a fun “campout” in the living room. Ahead of the storm, make sure your tent and sleeping bags are in good shape, or acquire these items if you don’t have them. Ensure you have plenty of heavy blankets, too. Then, when the power is out and temps in the house drop, set up the tent and unroll the sleeping bags. Body heat from people together in an enclosed space will help keep everyone warm. And you’ll have a fun story to tell!

If you’ve been meaning to caulk your windows, do it before cold weather strikes. Check the weatherstripping around your doors; odds are it’s seen better days. If your budget allows, replace or supplement your attic insulation. A less expensive way of sealing out some cold is to purchase some door draft stoppers, which you can tuck away in a closet until they are needed.

The worst time to buy a generator is the day you need one. If you live in an area that frequently loses power, consider purchasing a portable power station or a backup generator, which can be switched on manually or can automatically kick in when the power goes out. You can get generators powered by gasoline, natural gas, propane, or diesel (or even dual-fuel or inverter generators); solar generators are also an option but of course require a solar setup too.

After Testing 20 Air Purifiers, We Found One That Does Something the Rest Can’t

Same functionality, different package? Not with this Sans air purifier, which offers more advanced filtration and features than most models I’ve tested—without a premium price tag.

#7714. If You Commit a Crime with a Gun, You Might Not Want to Use a Purple Gun with a Blue Laser Sight

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

And if you do plan on doing that, you might not want to make a rap video depicting that very gun.

From Commonwealth v. Ashford, decided two weeks ago by a Pennsylvania appellate court, in an opinion by Judge Mary Murray, joined by Judges Timika Lane and Kate Ford Elliott:

The trial court summarized the evidence adduced at Appellant's jury trial …

On February 11, 2023, … [(Ms. South)] was carjacked in Reading City, Berks County, Pennsylvania, by three men in black balaclavas[, one of whom] brandish[ed a] handgun[ ] with blue laser sights….

The evening prior, on February 10, 2023, a video [("the video" or "the YouTube video")] was uploaded to the online video sharing platform[,] YouTube[,] depicting Appellant and [two] other men in black balaclavas handling and displaying various firearms with blue laser sights, including a purple Glock handgun. [The video was admitted into evidence and played for the jury at trial, albeit without sound.] The video itself is undated, though Appellant appears to be around the same age [in the video and at the time of the offense,] and is depicted wearing the same sweatshirt in which he was apprehended ten days later.

{The video, which is a part of the certified record, remains posted on YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W-IX9rvOflg (last visited Oct. 1, 2026); N.T., 5/15/25, Commonwealth Ex. 1. At several points during the two-minute-long video, Appellant (1) partially removes his facial covering, revealing his face; and (2) is holding a purple Glock handgun equipped with a blue laser sight. The video is accompanied by background music that was created by a rap musician with whom Appellant claims to have no association.} …

Approximately ten days later, on February 20, 2023, Officer Redinger of the Northwest Regional Police identified Ms. South's stolen car while on patrol in Mount Joy Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. When [Officer Redinger] attempted to pull the car over using lights and sirens, the vehicle fled. Several minutes later, law enforcement officers were eventually able to stop the fleeing vehicle using spike strips. Four male occupants, including Appellant, emerged and fled on foot in different directions[,] in pairs of two.

Sergeant [Seth] Arnold [(Sergeant Arnold)] of the Northwest Regional Police chased two of the males, including Appellant, behind a nearby residence. Sergeant Arnold was able to apprehend Appellant when [Appellant] tripped and fell near a trampoline in the backyard [of a residence].

When Sergeant Arnold retraced Appellant's path of flight, he observed a bright blue light shining in the grass near the trampoline. Closer inspection revealed the light to be emanating from a purple Glock handgun with a blue laser attachment….

Appellant contends the trial court's improper admission of the video violated his right to free expression ….

"[T]he government generally lacks the authority to restrict expression based on its message, topic, ideas, or content." Our Supreme Court has explained that "First Amendment freedoms apply broadly to different types of expression, including art, poetry, film, and music. Such freedoms apply equally to cultured, intellectual expressions and to crude, offensive, or tawdry ones." …

Here, the trial court determined that no violation of Appellant's right to free expression occurred by the admission of the video:

Necessarily, to raise a colorable claim under … the First Amendment …, speech itself must somehow be restricted or sanctioned by the government…. [In this case,] Neither the substantive lyrics nor expressive portrayals contained in the YouTube video at issue served as the basis for any of Appellant's criminal convictions. Saliently, Appellant's conviction for firearms not to be carried without a license did not stem from the depiction of Appellant displaying a firearm in the undated YouTube video. Rather, it was based on the totality of the circumstances indicating his power and intent to control the firearm in the early morning hours of February 20, 2023. The video was properly admitted solely to introduce its non-expressive aspects. Namely, it was highly probative of the fact that Appellant, having apparently constructively possessed the rare purple Glock with a blue laser sight shortly before the carjacking [of Ms. South], was likely to have continued to possess the weapon up to the point at which he discarded the weapon when fleeing from police ten days later. In short, because the artistic expressions contained in [the] video were not regulated or sanctioned by the Commonwealth in the instant matter, the free speech clauses of neither the federal nor the Pennsylvania Constitution were implicated by the admission of th[e] video at trial.

The trial court's reasoning is supported by the record, and its legal conclusion is sound. We conclude the trial court did not err in admitting the video, and Appellant's constitutional right to free expression was not implicated….

#7713. What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the New World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

How many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” says Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”

It’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”

For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”

This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

Composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they quickly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”

It’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

#7712. If You Run Social Media for a University, Don't Misprint the Nickname of Its Team

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Hinckley v. Univ. of Wyoming, decided Aug. 28 by Judge Scott Skavdahl (D. Wyo.), but just recently posted on Westlaw (appeal pending):

{Unless otherwise noted, these facts are uncontested.} Plaintiff … alleges that she was wrongfully terminated from her employment as a Marketing and Communications Specialist I at University of Wyoming because of her gender and in retaliation for protected workplace conduct….

Shortly after starting in her new role, Plaintiff began to display job performance issues, including being late to work, treating others poorly, and making mistakes. Some of these performance issues may have been due to the lack of oversight and direction supplied by [Marketing Manager] Cattelan, but Cattelan was not Plaintiff's supervisor. Nevertheless, Plaintiff made numerous mistakes that were not a result of Cattelan's lack of guidance or oversight.

For example, in November 2023, Plaintiff was asked to prepare a press release to celebrate a UW Professor who had received a national award. The professor met with Plaintiff, but found Plaintiff's draft inadequate due to "poor writing quality and lack of accuracy." Plaintiff responded combatively to the feedback and the press release was never published.

On December 8, 2023, Plaintiff posted the post [the first one in the image above -EV] to the College of Business' social media (Instagram). The post failed to meet College of Business brand standards and contained a significant spelling error, reading "Go Polks!" instead of "Go Pokes!" (hereinafter, the "first social media error"). Cattelan highlighted this error as particularly concerning given that Plaintiff is an alumna of the University of Wyoming….

For more, you can read the long opinion. But here's the heart of the matter, which is followed by the image that I placed at the top of the post:

Defendant has articulated several legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for Plaintiff's termination…. Plaintiff fails to show Defendant's stated reasons for terminating her were a mere pretext or that she incurred disparate treatment….

While Plaintiff disputes some of the characterization of these, the vast majority of incidents of Plaintiff's poor job performance are undisputed or admitted. She does not dispute the numerous social media errors were her fault. Plaintiff admits she received the university's brand book and she contends that her work followed the brand and voice of the College of Business.  Yet, no reasonable jury could find her social media posts adhered to COB brand guidelines. The failure to follow the brand guidelines is as simple as "Coca-Cola" versus "Pepsi" [a separate social media error that the court describes elsewhere -EV] or "Polks" v. "Pokes." …

#7711. The Best Dual-Fuel Generators for Home and Outdoor Use, Tested

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 16, 2026 7:25 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Dual-fuel generators offer the flexibility to run on either gasoline or propane, making them a versatile option for backup power. But with so many available, and many costing over $1,000, we tested a range of top models to help you find the right fit. Based on our results, we chose the Westinghouse WGen9500DF as our top pick for its powerful output, multiple starting options, and wide selection of outlets.

If you’re considering a dual-fuel generator but aren’t sure how much power you need or which features matter most, this guide can help. Below, we explain what to look for and share how five of the best dual-fuel generators performed in our hands-on tests.

Bottom line: Dual-fuel generators offer flexibility and power for home and outdoor use. Our tests highlight the best models to suit various needs and budgets.

Multifuel generators use gasoline or propane to provide electric power to your home, campground, or jobsite. But before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider whether it will meet your needs.

One key aspect of dual-fuel generators is you cannot run them indoors since they produce toxic fumes. Instead, you must set them up outside in a sheltered location and provide electrical power to appliances through an extension cord.

They are relatively heavy, weighing 100 to 200 pounds on average, and typically loud, sometimes exceeding the acceptable volumes allowed at RV parks. An inverter generator may be a better choice if you want a quiet generator. These generators have an enclosed body and supply power using a computer-controlled inverter instead of a noisier alternator.

However, if you need a decent amount of power, can see yourself regularly using more than one fuel type, and can handle a little extra weight and noise, a dual-fuel generator may be right for you.

The following dual-fuel generators represent the best the market has to offer in various categories. BobVila.com team members thoroughly tested each one, and we detail their pros and cons below.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4.5/5; Noise 4/5; Portability 4/5; Power 5/5; Value 4.5/5

When it comes to choosing a good all-around generator, it’s tough to beat the Westinghouse WGen9500DF. This powerful generator runs on gasoline or propane, and selecting one or the other is as simple as flipping a switch. The WGen9500DF comes with a 6.6-gallon gasoline tank that will power the unit for up to 12 hours at a 25 percent load.

Actual runtime will depend on gasoline quality and how much power you’re drawing. On propane, it can run up to 7 hours on a 20-pound tank when drawing a 50 percent load. This model has a 120/240V-50A outlet, a 120/240V-30A locking outlet, and four 120V-20A GFCI outlets. At 9,500 running watts on gasoline, it’s powerful enough to run several tools simultaneously as well as an oven/range combo and clothes dryer separately.

The downsides? At 211 pounds, this is a heavy generator. It’s also loud, comparable to a motorcycle, which is enough to annoy neighbors yet reasonable for its output. If you’re looking for a quiet model to use during a power outage, this might not be it. It is, however, a powerhouse of electrical output using whichever fuel is preferred.

What our tester says: “The remote-start key fob was my favorite feature—I could start the generator from a full 90 feet away once I put a fresh battery in the remote.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

When it comes to portable generators, 12,000 watts is near the top end in terms of power. For a propane generator ready to go at a moment’s notice, the Wen DF11000T is a great option. It provides slightly less power when operating on propane–9,500 peak watts and 7,500 running watts–but that’s still a lot of electrical power.

Before selecting several high-quality models for hands-on testing, we researched more than 24 dual-fuel generators, looking for quality construction, ease of use, portability, and power output. We gave some consideration to top manufacturers but didn’t automatically eliminate smaller or niche manufacturers if their generators were highly rated and competitively priced.

For actual testing, we assembled the generators and ran them according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We allotted time to models requiring break-in periods so the machines’ internal components could lubricate and settle before powering appliances or tools. Our team of testers then plugged in power tools, appliances, and more while using an online wattage calculator to estimate a suitable electrical load.

We awarded points to each model using a rubric considering ease of use, noise, portability, power, and value. The better a generator performed a test, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to determine top performers.

To find the best dual-fuel generator for your home, campground, or worksite, consider the factors listed below, including fuel efficiency, fuel tank capacity, power output, and control panel configuration.

Dual-fuel generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the fuel tank on the generator, the longer the generator can provide gasoline-based power. But, as tank size increases, so does the size of the generator.

Fuel capacity does not affect how much propane you can use with your dual-fuel generator. Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

The power output on dual-fuel generators is measured in watts. Manufacturers’ specs include peak power output and running power output. Peak power output refers to the maximum number of watts the generator can provide at any one time. Running power output equals the average number of watts produced during use.

Dual-fuel generators generally produce a power output from 1,000 watts to over 12,000 watts, depending on their size. Gasoline produces a higher wattage than propane, so many manufacturers of dual-fuel technology break wattage into propane peak and running outputs and gasoline peak and running outputs.

For greater power output needs, users may need to consider a standby generator rather than a portable dual-fuel option.

You can start your dual-fuel generator with an electric start switch or a recoil cord.

A generator’s operating noise level is measured in decibels. To understand the range of sound produced by a generator, consider these common sounds and their equivalent operating dB level:

Many dual-fuel generators produce 50 to 90 dB of noise, depending on fuel type (gasoline runs louder than propane) and power output. The most common range is between 65 dB and 75 dB, comparable to the sound of normal conversation.

The quietest dual-fuel generators combine dual-fuel technology and inverter technology to create a dual-fuel inverter generator.

Dual-fuel generators are typically large and heavy, with hoses or tanks that make them difficult to carry and move. Thus, some manufacturers include wheel kits for tilting the generator back and rolling it to the desired location.

You may also be able to purchase a wheel kit separately to add to your existing generator or replace an older wheel kit that doesn’t work well anymore. Either way, a wheel kit makes transporting a portable dual-fuel generator much easier.

Lift hook bars are handy on jobsites, allowing workers to attach the generator to a hook-and-pulley system and raise or lower it instead of carrying it up or down stairs or ladders. In industrial settings, this feature helps raise the generator onto a walkway or platform.

A lift hook bar will increase the generator’s weight (and likely the price), so don’t look for a generator with this feature unless you truly plan to use it.

Most dual-fuel generators are between 22 inches long by 22 inches wide by 22 inches high and 35 inches long by 30 inches wide by 30 inches high. They typically weigh between 100 and 250 pounds.

If you plan to move the generator frequently, figure size and weight prominently into your decision. Make sure the model you choose fits into your vehicle so you can transport it as needed. Remember, however, that larger, heavier motors are also the most powerful. You’ll want to find the right balance of size, weight, and power to meet your needs.

Gasoline and propane each have their pros and cons as fuel options. Gasoline is easier to find, but propane costs less. Propane is a better fuel source in hot summer weather, while gas burns better in the cold. A dual-fuel generator lets you choose one or the other based on immediate circumstances.

Using both fuel sources, one after the other, greatly increases a generator’s runtime. Users can run to the gas station to refuel while the generator keeps providing power on propane.

Before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider the answers to the following frequently asked questions.

A dual-fuel generator operates like a single-fuel generator, except it can burn propane and gasoline to produce electrical energy. It converts mechanical energy produced by the burning fuels to force the movement of electrical charges and generate electricity.

While some single-fuel generators can be adapted for use with natural gas, this isn’t the case with dual-fuel generators. Unless specially designed, dual-fuel generators do not run on natural gas and cannot be adapted for this purpose.

Propane gas is less expensive than gasoline, nearly impossible to spill, and burns cleaner, resulting in less wear on the engine over time. Running a dual-fuel generator on propane will save money but slightly decrease the machine’s peak and running watts.

Runtime is determined by fuel efficiency and fuel tank capacity. On average, a standard dual-fuel generator runs about 8 to 10 hours on propane.

If power is the goal, then the DuroMax dual-fuel generator is one of the best options to help ensure the campsite or essential home appliances have power for hours.

Depending on how much wattage a home draws under normal situations, attaching a high-capacity dual-fuel generator to its electrical system may be possible, but it’s not a DIY project.An electrician must install a transfer switch connecting the generator to the home’s electrical main. When the power goes out, the transfer switch automatically switches the incoming power from the grid to the generator. In most cases, the generator will be classified as a “standby generator” because it’s always ready to start generating electricity. Most portable generators are too small to run an entire home.

Generators running on gasoline are typically louder than those running on propane since burning propane requires less energy.

As with most outdoor tools and large household appliances, you will want to take dual-fuel generators to a local recycling plant for recycling.

#7710. Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

Unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can quickly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”

Vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can quickly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception issue if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty says. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”

Fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be new to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker says. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”

Adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker says. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”

While low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes says.  But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty says. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland says. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland says. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our new neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty says. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

#7708. Arkansas S. Ct.: Legislature May Revive Cases Barred by Statute of Limitations

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court reverses its precedent, dating back to 1846, that held such revival unconstitutionally restricted the defendant's "vested rights" not to be sued, which had been created by the earlier statute of limitations.

From H.C. v. Nesmith, decided last week by the Arkansas Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Nicholas Bronni, joined by Justices Courtney Rae Hudson, Cody Hiland, and Rhonda Wood (note that other state courts are split on this question, see, e.g., this post and this one):

This case presents a particularly important question: Can the General Assembly extend the statute of limitations in cases where it has already run and afford child-sex-abuse victims an opportunity to hold their abusers accountable? … [T]his court's vested-rights precedent … categorically bars "expand[ing] a limitation period so as to revive a claim already barred." …

Revisiting our vested-rights precedent, we conclude that it lacks any constitutional basis and, as such, cannot stand. We therefore overrule our prior cases prohibiting the legislature from expanding a limitations period and thereby reviving time-barred claims [and] uphold the Vulnerable Victims of Sex Abuse Act against Nesmith's constitutional challenge ….

[Under] our vested-rights precedent …, "the legislature cannot expand a statute of limitation so as to revive a cause of action already barred." That doctrine rests on the assumption that when a civil statute of limitations runs, a tortfeasor has a vested right to the property that could have been the subject of a potential claim….

[But] our cases do not cite any constitutional basis for that doctrine. Far from it, when we first employed that principle to strike down legislation in 1933, we instead relied on a single legal encyclopedia published in 1915 assuring us that—at that sole moment in time—most jurisdictions held that legislatures could not revive a claim after a statute-of-limitations defense had run. Or, perhaps more generously, we relied on that legal encyclopedia plus an unreasoned extension of this court's prior case law suggesting that to retroactively alter an applicable statute of limitations, the legislature needed to speak clearly and show it had considered the consequences. That approach, unbound by actual text or constitutional history, is not consistent with our constitutional role….

To be sure, some later cases—perhaps recognizing that our earlier cases do not cite any constitutional language supporting our vested-rights precedent—suggest that precedent rests on due-process principles…. [But] that label does not work because the expiration of a statute-of-limitations period does not confer a property right—or any other right for that matter.

As the Supreme Court has explained in rejecting similar arguments under the federal due process clause, a statute-of-limitations period merely governs the time within which a claim must be brought, see Chase Sec. Corp. v. Donaldson (1945); it does not reflect a legislative judgment "that [a] defendant should 'be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time.'" Instead, these limitations "are by definition arbitrary" and rest entirely on legislative judgments about how best to encourage plaintiffs to diligently pursue claims and avoid litigation "after memories have faded, witnesses have died or disappeared, and evidence has been lost."

As such, they "represent a public policy [choice] about" how to balance those interests and exist only by "legislative grace." Altering that period and establishing a different, equally "arbitrary" date does not—contrary to our prior case law's unfounded assertion—deprive a defendant of any vested property right. Rather, balancing competing interests and "resolv[ing] the debate" about when a claim should be time-barred is precisely the kind of thing that our constitution leaves "to the legislature."

We therefore hold that the court's vested-rights precedent has no basis in law, and we overrule our prior cases categorically barring the legislature from expanding the limitations period and thereby reviving claims. Indeed, as we recently reaffirmed, "we are bound by constitutional text," not precedent that "treats our constitution not as a written document but as a set of civic values and norms determined by judges." And we now restore to the General Assembly its constitutional power to decide how long is too long to bring a claim….

Recognizing the vital importance of stare decisis, I nonetheless conclude that this is an exceptional case that warrants breaking with our precedent. Before the General Assembly enacted the Justice for Vulnerable Victims of Sexual Abuse Act, victims of sexual abuse who were under age twenty-one generally had until three years after attaining full age to file suit. Yet childhood sexual abuse presents a unique problem in that—by its very nature—it often prevents victims from bringing timely claims. This consideration leads me to conclude that great injury and injustice will result if we continue to follow our vested-rights precedent in this case….

In recent years, research has revealed the prevalence of childhood sexual abuse and some of the reasons for delayed reporting. For example, we now know that at least one in four girls and one in twenty boys in the United States experience child sexual abuse. Even still, childhood sexual abuse is vastly underreported, and when it is reported, often years or decades have passed. Victims may be reluctant to come forward due to the negative repercussions of disclosure, such as disruptions in family stability, loss of close relationships, or involvement with the authorities; fear of not being believed; and psychological obstacles such as shame and self-blame….

I disagree with the majority's decision to upend 180 years of this court's precedent prohibiting legislative attempts to revive expired statutes of limitation…. In my view, applying our vested-rights precedent to the present case, … the legislature lacked the power to revive the expired statute of limitations applicable to Nesmith, and therefore, the claims against Nesmith were time-barred.

[I]n 1846 this court in Couch v. McKee treated the completed bar [of the statute of limitations] as a property interest that cannot be removed by later legislation. When the statute has run, the defendant's right to be free from the claim becomes part of his or her protected legal estate, an interest the State cannot simply reassign by retroactive enactment. Our later cases have repeatedly applied that same rule, holding that revival statutes cannot constitutionally divest a defendant of a vested limitations defense.

Nor, contrary to the majority's assertion, is our vested-rights jurisprudence untethered from constitutional text. The Arkansas Constitution reflects a longstanding hostility toward retroactive laws impairing settled rights. See Ark. Const. art. 2, § 17 (prohibiting ex post facto laws and laws impairing contractual obligations); id. § 21 (protecting due process). Consistent with those principles, this court has repeatedly recognized that retroactive legislation may not constitutionally disturb vested substantive rights….

That rule is not a mere formalism. Statutes of limitation serve an important public function. They encourage the prompt filing of claims so that the truth-finding process is not impaired by faded memories, lost documents, unavailable records, and deceased witnesses. Those concerns are not hypothetical. The amicus brief filed in this case illustrates the serious prejudice that can result when claims are revived decades after the fact.

Ms. Shirley Suhl, an eighty-seven-year-old retired widow, represents that she is defending claims in federal court arising from alleged events at a facility that ceased operating around 2006 and from conduct dating back nearly forty years. She is not alleged to have personally committed sexual abuse; rather, she is alleged to have known of or been complicit in abuse by others. According to her brief, relevant facility records no longer exist, potential witnesses are elderly or deceased, and one named former employee accused of abuse is now in his nineties. Whether those allegations ultimately have merit is not before us. The point is more basic: the passage of decades can make a fair defense difficult, sometimes impossible.

This is precisely why Arkansas law has treated an accrued limitations defense as vested. Once the limitations period has run, the defendant is entitled to repose, not because the underlying allegations are unimportant but because the law recognizes that, at some point, the defense of stale claims becomes too impaired to permit reliable adjudication. The majority treats the limitations bar as a revocable act of legislative grace. Our cases have treated it differently. They have recognized that once the bar attaches, it becomes a substantive right to resist enforcement of the claim. That rule does not deny the gravity of child sexual abuse. It enforces the constitutional limit on retroactive legislation that destroys vested rights.

In this instance, stare decisis carries particular force. The rule the majority abandons today is not isolated or recently decided precedent. It can be traced back to this court's earliest jurisprudence and has been reaffirmed across generations of cases. Litigants, lawyers, and the General Assembly have long operated against that settled backdrop. Yet today, the majority discards nearly two centuries of precedent. Stability in the law matters, especially when the court alters longstanding rules governing substantive rights and retroactive legislation….

{While many judges and justices pledge full allegiance to the doctrine of stare decisis, even to the point of perpetuating clear errors of constitutional interpretation, I am not one of them. And while it is an important piece of our judicial system, I have frequently noted that "[t]his court "should not invoke stare decisis to uphold precedents that are demonstrably erroneous." Here, however, our two centuries of case law on the subject are rooted in the Arkansas Constitution as article 2 section 21 supports our precedent. Accordingly, I would follow it.

Joshua D. Gillispie (Gillispie Law Firm) and Brian G. Brooks represent plaintiffs.
